techniques.name: Lead with the why
techniques.summary: Open a direction-setting conversation with the purpose behind the work before the what and the how, so people can make their own trade-offs.
techniques.how_to_apply: Before assigning work or announcing a change, say in one or two sentences what outcome it serves and why it matters to customers, the business or the team. Then the what, then the how.
techniques.drill: For the next five requests Tom makes, start each with 'The reason this matters is...' and keep it under 20 words.

techniques.name: Paint a concrete picture of success
techniques.summary: Describe what the future looks like when the goal is met, in specific and sensory terms, rather than abstract aims.
techniques.how_to_apply: When setting a goal, describe a day or a customer moment in the future state: who is doing what, what has changed, what number moved.
techniques.drill: Write a three-sentence 'day in the life after we win' for Tom's current top priority and use it to open the next team meeting.

sources.where: Why do we exist / What are we going to do

techniques.name: One thematic goal for now
techniques.summary: Name a single, time-bound rallying priority that everyone on the leadership team shares, on top of their normal jobs.
techniques.how_to_apply: Agree one qualitative goal for the next few months, plus a handful of defining objectives, and review progress against it at every leadership meeting.
techniques.drill: At the start of each leadership meeting this month, state the thematic goal and ask for one red/amber/green on it from each person.

techniques.name: Say what we will not do
techniques.summary: Make strategy real by naming the things the team will stop or decline, not just the things it will do.
techniques.how_to_apply: With every priority, name at least one thing that is deprioritised or stopped, and say who will tell affected stakeholders.
techniques.drill: For each priority Tom sets this week, add one 'and therefore we will not...' sentence.

techniques.name: State commander's intent
techniques.summary: Give the purpose, the desired end state and the key constraints, so people can act sensibly when the plan meets reality.
techniques.how_to_apply: When briefing, cover three things: the purpose, what done looks like, and the limits (budget, risk, deadlines). Leave the method to the team.
techniques.drill: Before the next delegation, write the intent in three lines (purpose, end state, limits) and read it out.

techniques.name: Set specific, stretching goals
techniques.summary: Specific, challenging goals tend to beat 'do your best' because they focus effort and allow progress to be measured.
techniques.how_to_apply: Turn vague aims into a measurable outcome with a date and a level that is hard but believable; agree how progress will be seen.
techniques.drill: Rewrite each goal Tom states in his next three meetings as 'from X to Y by when'.

techniques.name: Technical or adaptive?
techniques.summary: Distinguish problems experts can fix from problems that need people to change their habits, values or loyalties, and lead each differently.
techniques.how_to_apply: Ask aloud whether a known fix exists. If not, treat it as adaptive: involve the people affected, expect discomfort, and do not hand down a solution.
techniques.drill: Pick the three hardest open issues; for each, Tom states aloud in the meeting whether it is technical or adaptive and why.

techniques.name: Get on the balcony
techniques.summary: Step back mid-discussion to observe the pattern of the conversation and the system, not just the content.
techniques.how_to_apply: When a discussion loops or heats up, pause and describe what is happening ('we keep coming back to X; maybe the real issue is Y'), then ask if others see it.
techniques.drill: In each meeting, make one 'balcony' observation about the pattern of the conversation and check it with the group.

techniques.name: Confront the brutal facts with faith
techniques.summary: Combine plain acknowledgement of the hardest facts with steady confidence that the team will prevail.
techniques.how_to_apply: State the worst current facts without softening, then state why you believe the team can still win and what you'll do.
techniques.drill: When next reporting bad news, use two sentences: 'The facts are...' and 'What I believe and will do is...'.

techniques.name: Label facts, assumptions and judgements
techniques.sub_capability: Thinking out loud: assumptions and trade-offs
techniques.summary: When explaining a view, say which parts are known, which are assumed and which are judgement, so others can test the weak links.
techniques.how_to_apply: Use explicit tags while reasoning aloud: 'the fact is', 'I'm assuming', 'my judgement is'. Ask which assumption others would challenge first.
techniques.drill: In the next strategy discussion, Tom names his top two assumptions out loud and asks the group to attack them.

techniques.name: Speak in probabilities
techniques.sub_capability: Thinking out loud: assumptions and trade-offs
techniques.summary: Express uncertain judgements as likelihoods rather than certainties, which invites calibration and better debate.
techniques.how_to_apply: Replace 'this will work' with a rough percentage and the reason; invite others to give their own number before discussing.
techniques.drill: For one week, every forecast Tom gives in a meeting includes a percentage; review hit rates monthly.

techniques.name: Model the reasoning, not just the answer
techniques.sub_capability: Thinking out loud: assumptions and trade-offs
techniques.summary: Share how you got to a view (criteria, options rejected, what would change your mind), so the team learns to think strategically.
techniques.how_to_apply: After giving a conclusion, spend a minute on the path: what you weighed, what you dropped and why, and what evidence would change your mind.
techniques.drill: After each decision Tom announces, add one sentence of 'what would change my mind'.

techniques.name: Diagnose the situation type
techniques.summary: Different business situations (start-up, turnaround, accelerated growth, realignment, sustaining success) call for different priorities and leadership styles.
techniques.how_to_apply: In a new role or initiative, name aloud which situation each part of the portfolio is in and what that implies for pace and style.
techniques.drill: List Tom's three main areas, label each STARS type, and share it with his boss to check agreement.

techniques.name: Agree expectations with the boss early
techniques.summary: Hold explicit conversations with the boss on the situation, expectations, working style, resources and personal development.
techniques.how_to_apply: Plan the topics across early 1:1s with the boss and check alignment on what success looks like and by when.
techniques.drill: Book five boss conversations over a month, one per theme, and record a one-line agreement after each.

techniques.name: Name who has the D
techniques.summary: For each significant decision, make clear who recommends, who must agree, who gives input, who decides and who carries it out.
techniques.how_to_apply: When a decision item opens, say who decides and what role everyone else in the room plays. If it isn't clear, settle that first.
techniques.drill: For the next three cross-team decisions, write the R, A, P, I and D roles in the meeting note before discussion starts.

techniques.name: Say which decision style you're using
techniques.summary: Tell people whether you are informing them of a decision, consulting them before you decide, or asking them to decide together, so input isn't mistaken for a vote.
techniques.how_to_apply: Before discussion, state the mode: 'I've decided, here's why'; 'I'll decide after hearing you'; or 'we'll decide together'. Stick to it.
techniques.drill: In every decision item for two weeks, Tom states the mode in his first sentence.

techniques.name: Widen beyond whether-or-not
techniques.summary: Decisions framed as a single yes/no option tend to fail more often than those weighing several alternatives.
techniques.how_to_apply: When a proposal arrives as 'should we do X?', ask for at least one genuine alternative and a 'what if we couldn't do X?' option before judging.
techniques.drill: For each decision this month, Tom asks 'what's option two?' before anyone argues for option one.

techniques.name: Agree criteria before preferences
techniques.summary: Settle how options will be judged before people state which they prefer, reducing motivated reasoning.
techniques.how_to_apply: List two to four criteria and their rough weights, then score the options, then discuss preferences.
techniques.drill: On the next significant decision, write criteria on the whiteboard before options are discussed.

techniques.name: Speak last on contested calls
techniques.summary: When the leader states a view first, others tend to anchor on it or fall silent; holding back until others speak surfaces more information.
techniques.how_to_apply: On contested items, ask each person for their view before giving your own; say explicitly that you'll share yours last.
techniques.drill: In the next five team decisions, the coach checks whether Tom's first opinion comes after at least two others.

techniques.name: Collect independent views first
techniques.summary: Ask people to form and record their judgement independently before group discussion, so the group gets genuinely separate estimates.
techniques.how_to_apply: Before a decision meeting, ask for written views or scores; in the room, have everyone note their answer before anyone speaks.
techniques.drill: For the next forecast or estimate, run a silent-write round before discussion and compare spread.

techniques.name: Ask for the strongest case against
techniques.summary: Explicitly invite the best argument against the favoured option; genuine dissent improves decision quality more than role-played dissent.
techniques.how_to_apply: Before converging, ask: 'What's the strongest case against this?' and 'Who disagrees, even partly?' Reward the person who answers.
techniques.drill: In each decision item, Tom asks for the case against at least once and summarises it fairly before deciding.

techniques.name: Run a pre-mortem
techniques.summary: Imagine the decision has failed and ask everyone to write the reasons why, which surfaces risks people otherwise keep quiet about.
techniques.how_to_apply: Before committing, say: 'It's a year from now and this has failed. Take two minutes and write why.' Collect reasons and adjust the plan.
techniques.drill: Run a ten-minute pre-mortem on the next project before kick-off; the coach checks for at least three new risks and an owner per mitigation.

techniques.name: Weigh views by track record
techniques.summary: Give more weight to people with relevant track records and clear reasoning, while still hearing everyone.
techniques.how_to_apply: When views conflict, ask each person about their experience with this type of decision and their reasoning; weigh accordingly and say so.
techniques.drill: On the next contested call, Tom asks each contributor 'how many times have you seen this play out?' before weighing views.

techniques.name: Two-way doors move fast
techniques.summary: Separate reversible decisions, which should be made quickly by small groups, from hard-to-reverse ones that deserve a slow, careful process.
techniques.how_to_apply: Ask aloud: 'Can we undo this cheaply?' If yes, decide now with roughly 70 percent of the information. If no, slow down and widen input.
techniques.drill: Tag every decision in Tom's meetings this week as one-way or two-way and track time-to-decision.

techniques.name: Decide or set the decision date
techniques.summary: Avoid open-ended deferral: either decide now or name what information is missing, who gets it, and when the decision will be made.
techniques.how_to_apply: If you can't decide in the meeting, say what would make it decidable, assign it, and set the date and decider.
techniques.drill: For each deferred item, Tom must say 'missing info, owner, decision date'; the coach flags any deferral without all three.

techniques.name: State the decision in one sentence
techniques.summary: Close each decision item with a clear sentence of what was decided, so nobody leaves with a different version.
techniques.how_to_apply: End the item with 'So we've decided...' plus any key condition, and ask if anyone heard it differently.
techniques.drill: The coach counts decision items with a closing decision sentence; target 100 percent for two weeks.

techniques.name: Disagree and commit
techniques.summary: After real debate, people who disagreed commit fully to the decision; the leader can model this by committing to calls they argued against.
techniques.how_to_apply: Once a decision is made, ask dissenters explicitly whether they can commit, and say you will back it in front of others.
techniques.drill: After each contested decision, Tom asks each dissenter 'can you commit to this?' and notes the answer.

techniques.name: Judge the decision, not the outcome
techniques.summary: A bad outcome does not prove a bad decision; review the information, process and judgement separately from luck.
techniques.how_to_apply: In reviews, ask what was knowable at the time, whether the process was sound, and what part was luck, before assigning credit or blame.
techniques.drill: In the next post-mortem, Tom splits the discussion into 'what we knew', 'how we decided', 'what was luck'.

techniques.name: Keep a decision journal
techniques.summary: Record major decisions with the reasoning, expected outcome and confidence at the time, to learn honestly later.
techniques.how_to_apply: For significant calls, note in two minutes: the decision, options, expected result, confidence, and what would make it wrong. Review quarterly.
techniques.drill: Start a decision log; Tom adds one entry per week and reviews the first batch in three months.

techniques.name: Who does what by when
techniques.summary: Every agreed action gets one named owner, a concrete deliverable and a date, spoken aloud and confirmed.
techniques.how_to_apply: When an action comes up, stop and pin it: name, verb, deliverable, date. Ask the owner to confirm out loud.
techniques.drill: The coach counts actions in Tom's meetings and flags any without owner and date; target is zero gaps for a fortnight.

techniques.name: Turn intentions into if-then plans
techniques.summary: Commitments stated as 'when X happens, I will do Y' are more likely to be carried out than general intentions.
techniques.how_to_apply: When someone commits, help them name the trigger and the first step: when and where they'll start, and what they'll do if blocked.
techniques.drill: In 1:1s this month, for each new commitment Tom asks 'when exactly will you start, and what's step one?'.

techniques.name: Get the owner to say it back
techniques.summary: Ask the owner to restate the action in their own words; misunderstandings surface before work starts.
techniques.how_to_apply: After assigning, ask: 'Can you play back what you're taking away?' Correct any gaps there and then.
techniques.drill: In the next five delegations, Tom asks for a playback and notes any mismatch.

techniques.name: Open with last time's actions
techniques.summary: Start recurring meetings by reviewing the commitments from the previous one, owner by owner, briefly and without drama.
techniques.how_to_apply: First five minutes: read the action list, ask each owner done / not done / new date. Explore misses after the review, not during.
techniques.drill: For a month, every meeting Tom chairs starts with the previous action list; the coach checks the first five minutes.

techniques.name: Make progress visible against goals
techniques.summary: Regularly review progress on a small set of goals with the team, so people can see where they stand.
techniques.how_to_apply: Pick the two or three measures that matter, review them in the same order every week, and ask what the trend means for actions.
techniques.drill: Choose three team measures; Tom reviews them first in each weekly meeting for six weeks.

techniques.name: Own it first
techniques.summary: When something goes wrong in Tom's area, he takes responsibility publicly before discussing others' parts.
techniques.how_to_apply: Open failure discussions with what Tom could have done differently (briefing, resourcing, follow-up), then move to fixes.
techniques.drill: In each review of a miss, Tom's first statement names one thing he'll do differently; the coach checks the first Tom turn.

techniques.name: No bad teams, check the briefing
techniques.summary: Treat a team's poor performance first as a question about the leader's clarity, priorities and support.
techniques.how_to_apply: Before criticising execution, ask the team: 'What wasn't clear from me? What did you need that you didn't get?'
techniques.drill: After the next missed deadline, Tom asks his team two questions about his own briefing before anything else.

sources.where: no bad teams, only bad leaders

techniques.name: Name the gap, then ask
techniques.summary: When a commitment is missed, describe the expected and actual result factually, then ask what happened before judging.
techniques.how_to_apply: State: 'We agreed X by Tuesday; it's not done.' Then ask an open question and listen. Diagnose whether it's motivation or ability, then agree the fix.
techniques.drill: The next time a commitment is missed, Tom uses the gap-then-question pattern within the same meeting; the coach checks the wording.

techniques.name: Diagnose motivation vs ability
techniques.summary: Work out whether a miss is about willingness or capability (or the system), because each needs a different response.
techniques.how_to_apply: Ask about obstacles and skills before assuming lack of effort: 'Is this about time, know-how, or something else?'
techniques.drill: In each accountability conversation, Tom asks one question about ability and one about obstacles before suggesting a fix.

techniques.name: Agree the consequence and check-in
techniques.summary: End accountability conversations with an explicit plan, a check-in date and, where needed, what happens if it slips again.
techniques.how_to_apply: Close with: new commitment, how Tom will check, and the consequence if missed, stated calmly.
techniques.drill: For the next three accountability conversations, the coach checks the last minute for date, check-in and consequence.

techniques.name: Peer accountability in the room
techniques.summary: Encourage team members to hold each other to commitments rather than routing everything through the leader.
techniques.how_to_apply: When one team member's miss affects another, invite the affected peer to say so directly in the meeting, and model doing it respectfully.
techniques.drill: In the next team meeting, Tom hands at least one cross-team dependency to the two peers to resolve in the room.

techniques.name: Run a quick after-action review
techniques.summary: After a milestone or setback, ask what was meant to happen, what happened, why, and what to do differently; structured debriefs reliably improve performance.
techniques.how_to_apply: Run the four questions within days of the event, keep it to 15-30 minutes, focus on process not blame, and end with one or two changes with owners.
techniques.drill: After the next milestone, Tom runs a 20-minute after-action review; the coach checks the four questions and a closing action.

techniques.name: Blameless curiosity about mistakes
techniques.summary: Separate blameworthy acts from honest errors and complex-system failures, and respond to the latter with curiosity.
techniques.how_to_apply: Ask 'what made that seem like the right move at the time?' and 'what in the system made this easy to get wrong?'
techniques.drill: In the next incident review, Tom asks at least two system questions before any question about individual decisions.

techniques.name: From 'can I' to 'I intend to'
techniques.summary: Shift reports from asking permission to stating what they intend to do, so they do the thinking and the leader only approves or questions.
techniques.how_to_apply: When asked 'should I...?' or 'can I...?', reply 'tell me what you intend to do'. Over time, ask them to come with intentions, not questions.
techniques.drill: For a month, whenever a report asks permission, Tom replies with 'what do you intend to do?'; the coach tracks the shift in reports' language.

techniques.name: Delegate the decision, not just the task
techniques.summary: Hand over authority for the outcome along with the work, with clear limits, rather than retaining every call.
techniques.how_to_apply: Say explicitly which decisions the person owns and which still need Tom, and resist taking them back.
techniques.drill: In each delegation this week, Tom states 'you decide X; I decide Y'.

techniques.name: Use the ladder of involvement
techniques.summary: Make the level of delegation explicit: from 'tell me what's happening' through 'recommend', 'decide and tell me', to 'decide, no need to tell me'.
techniques.how_to_apply: When handing something over, say which level applies and when it will move up.
techniques.drill: Tom labels each delegated item with a level for two weeks; reports confirm they heard it.

techniques.name: Adjust to task-relevant maturity
techniques.summary: The right amount of direction depends on how experienced the person is with this particular task, not their seniority overall.
techniques.how_to_apply: Before delegating, ask the person how often they've done this; give structure for novices and space for experts, and say what you're doing.
techniques.drill: Before each delegation, Tom asks one experience question and states how closely he'll be involved.

techniques.name: Agree the check-in rhythm up front
techniques.summary: Set how and when progress will be checked at the start, so follow-up feels planned rather than intrusive.
techniques.how_to_apply: When delegating, agree the first check-in date and what you want to see, and drop ad hoc 'any update?' requests.
techniques.drill: Every delegation Tom makes for two weeks includes a named first check-in.

techniques.name: Don't take the monkey
techniques.summary: When someone brings a problem, help them own the next step instead of taking the problem away.
techniques.how_to_apply: Ask 'what do you think we should do?' and 'what's your next step?' before offering to act. End with the action sitting with them.
techniques.drill: The coach counts actions Tom volunteers to take in 1:1s; aim to halve them over a month.

techniques.name: Ask before you answer
techniques.summary: Leaders who answer every question train teams to stop thinking; asking first develops judgement and surfaces better ideas.
techniques.how_to_apply: When asked for an answer, ask one question first ('what are you leaning towards?'). Answer only if they're stuck or it's urgent.
techniques.drill: For one week, Tom's first response to every 'what should I do' is a question; the coach checks.

techniques.name: Explain the why and offer choice
techniques.summary: Leaders who give rationale, offer choices and acknowledge others' views tend to have more motivated and better-performing people.
techniques.how_to_apply: When asking for something, give the reason, offer a choice where possible (how, when, which first), and acknowledge any constraint the person faces.
techniques.drill: In 1:1s for two weeks, every request Tom makes includes a reason and, where possible, a choice.

techniques.name: Acknowledge their perspective before directing
techniques.summary: Show you understand the other person's view or constraint before asking them to do something different.
techniques.how_to_apply: Briefly reflect their position ('I know this lands on top of the audit'), then make the ask.
techniques.drill: Tom precedes his next five directive requests with one sentence acknowledging the person's situation.

techniques.name: Offer a stretch with backing
techniques.summary: Give people challenges a little beyond what they've done, make the stretch explicit and say why you think they can do it.
techniques.how_to_apply: Name the stretch, the reason you chose them, and the support available; let them present the outcome themselves.
techniques.drill: Over a month, the coach counts how often reports present their own work in Tom's meetings vs Tom presenting it.

techniques.name: Ask for the big question, not the answer
techniques.summary: Frame a challenge as a question or opportunity the team must work out, rather than handing down a solution.
techniques.how_to_apply: Describe the challenge and why it matters, ask the team how they'd tackle it, and let them fill the gap.
techniques.drill: Next planning session: Tom frames one challenge purely as a question and doesn't offer an answer for 15 minutes.

techniques.name: Start with 'what's on your mind?'
techniques.summary: Open coaching conversations with a broad, focused question that lets the other person choose what matters most.
techniques.how_to_apply: Begin 1:1s with an open question about their priorities, then let them lead; don't start with your own list.
techniques.drill: In every 1:1 for a month, Tom's first question is open and he lets the report choose the topic.

techniques.name: And what else?
techniques.summary: The first answer is rarely the whole story; a simple follow-up prompt draws out more options and the real issue.
techniques.how_to_apply: After someone answers, ask 'and what else?' two or three times before moving on.
techniques.drill: In the next three 1:1s, Tom uses 'and what else?' at least twice; the coach checks for new content afterwards.

techniques.name: Find the real challenge
techniques.summary: Help people focus on the core issue for them, rather than solving the first problem they mention.
techniques.how_to_apply: Ask 'what's the real challenge here for you?' and stay with the person's own part of it.
techniques.drill: Use the focus question in each coaching conversation this week before giving any input.

techniques.name: Ask more, follow up more
techniques.summary: People who ask more questions, especially follow-ups, are liked more and learn more; leaders underestimate this.
techniques.how_to_apply: Aim for most of Tom's turns in a 1:1 to be questions, and make most of those build on what the person just said.
techniques.drill: The coach reports Tom's question share and follow-up count after each 1:1; aim for at least half of his turns as questions.

techniques.name: Stay curious a little longer
techniques.summary: Delay giving advice; the urge to fix often leads to solving the wrong problem and undercuts the other person's thinking.
techniques.how_to_apply: Before offering a view, ask at least three questions. When you do advise, say it's one option and ask what they think.
techniques.drill: In 1:1s, the coach measures how long until Tom's first piece of advice; aim to double it.

techniques.name: Don't add too much value
techniques.summary: Leaders tend to add their tweak to others' ideas, which lowers the person's ownership more than it improves the idea.
techniques.how_to_apply: When someone brings a decent idea, say 'go for it' or ask one question, rather than adding improvements.
techniques.drill: For a week, Tom notes each time he adds to an idea; the coach flags 'great, but' turns.

techniques.name: Their meeting, not yours
techniques.summary: Regular 1:1s should be driven by the report's agenda, with the manager listening most of the time.
techniques.how_to_apply: Ask the report to bring topics; let them talk most of the time; hold Tom's items until the end.
techniques.drill: The coach reports Tom's talk share for every 1:1; aim below 0.4.

techniques.name: Ask what's getting in the way
techniques.summary: Regularly ask about obstacles and whether the manager is part of the problem, then remove blockers.
techniques.how_to_apply: In each 1:1, ask 'what's slowing you down?' and 'is there anything I'm doing that makes it harder?'.
techniques.drill: Add the blocker question to every 1:1 for a month; the coach checks follow-through in the next 1:1.

sources.where: lazy question: how can I help?

techniques.name: Check in on the person, not just the work
techniques.summary: Start or end 1:1s with genuine interest in how the person is doing; trust and engagement depend on it.
techniques.how_to_apply: Ask a real personal question and listen to the answer before work topics.
techniques.drill: Tom opens each 1:1 with a personal question and follows up on what he heard last time.

techniques.name: Career conversation in three parts
techniques.summary: Understand someone's life story and values, their dreams, and the skills they need next, then link current work to that path.
techniques.how_to_apply: Hold a dedicated conversation: what's shaped you, where do you want to be, what do you need to learn. Refer back to it in later 1:1s.
techniques.drill: Hold one career conversation with each direct report this quarter; the coach checks later 1:1s for references to their goals.

techniques.name: Ask what was most useful
techniques.summary: End coaching conversations by asking what the person found most useful, which reinforces learning and gives feedback to the coach.
techniques.how_to_apply: Close with: 'What was most useful about this?' and listen.
techniques.drill: End every 1:1 for two weeks with the learning question.

techniques.name: Teach the thinking behind the call
techniques.summary: Develop people's judgement by explaining how you reached a decision, then giving them the next similar one.
techniques.how_to_apply: After explaining a call, say 'next time this comes up, you make it, and run it past me'.
techniques.drill: After each decision that a report could learn from, Tom adds one hand-over sentence.

techniques.name: Coaching style when people want to grow
techniques.summary: Coaching works when the person is open to developing; with someone resistant or in a crisis, other styles fit better.
techniques.how_to_apply: Before coaching, check the person wants to work on this; if not, switch to direct feedback or direction and say so.
techniques.drill: Before starting a coaching conversation, Tom asks one readiness question.

techniques.name: Praise the behaviour and its effect
techniques.summary: Specific recognition of what someone did and the difference it made is more useful and believable than generic praise.
techniques.how_to_apply: Name the action, the result, and why it mattered, soon after it happens.
techniques.drill: In each team meeting, Tom gives one specific piece of praise naming behaviour and effect.

techniques.name: Situation, behaviour, impact
techniques.summary: Describe the situation, the observable behaviour and its impact, rather than judging the person's character.
techniques.how_to_apply: Use three short parts: when and where, what they did (camera view), and what effect it had. Then ask for their view.
techniques.drill: For the next three pieces of critical feedback, the coach checks for situation, behaviour, impact and a question.

techniques.name: Care personally, challenge directly
techniques.summary: Good feedback shows care for the person and is direct about the problem; avoiding the challenge out of niceness lets people fail.
techniques.how_to_apply: Say the hard thing plainly and briefly, and make the care visible (why you're telling them, offer of help).
techniques.drill: Before each difficult feedback conversation, Tom writes the one-sentence message and the coach checks it was said within the first two minutes.

techniques.name: Skip the feedback sandwich
techniques.summary: Wrapping criticism between praise tends to bury the message and make future praise suspect.
techniques.how_to_apply: Keep praise and criticism separate; state the criticism clearly on its own and check it landed.
techniques.drill: The coach flags sandwich patterns in Tom's feedback turns for a month.

techniques.name: Keep feedback on the task, not the self
techniques.summary: Feedback that draws attention to the person's self-image rather than the task often lowers performance.
techniques.how_to_apply: Focus on the work, the gap and how to close it; avoid comments about personality or comparisons with others.
techniques.drill: Review three recent feedback moments with the coach and rewrite any person-focused lines as task-focused.

techniques.name: Ask for criticism and embrace the discomfort
techniques.summary: Leaders who ask for criticism first make candour safer for everyone; the ask must be specific and the silence tolerated.
techniques.how_to_apply: Ask a specific question ('what's one thing I could do differently in these meetings?'), then wait at least six seconds, then thank and act.
techniques.drill: Once a week, Tom asks one specific feedback question in a 1:1 and counts to six before speaking.

techniques.name: Thank, don't defend
techniques.summary: When receiving criticism, the leader's reaction teaches the team whether candour is safe.
techniques.how_to_apply: Respond with thanks and a clarifying question; hold any explanation for later; say what you'll do.
techniques.drill: The coach flags every 'yes, but' in Tom's response to criticism for a month.

techniques.name: Ask for feedforward
techniques.summary: Ask for suggestions for the future rather than critiques of the past, which people find easier to give and receive.
techniques.how_to_apply: Ask: 'What are two things I could do next month to be better at X?' Listen, thank, don't argue.
techniques.drill: Tom asks three colleagues for feedforward on one behaviour this month.

techniques.name: Two-minute feedback right after
techniques.summary: Short, immediate feedback after a meeting or moment is more useful than saving it up for formal reviews.
techniques.how_to_apply: Within a day of seeing something worth comment, give a one- or two-minute piece of feedback in private.
techniques.drill: Tom gives two impromptu feedback moments a week; the coach checks they reference the same or previous day.

techniques.name: Wise feedback: high bar plus belief
techniques.summary: Critical feedback is more likely to be accepted and acted on when it states high standards and confidence the person can meet them.
techniques.how_to_apply: Before or after critical comments, say plainly that the bar is high and you believe they can reach it.
techniques.drill: Add a standards-and-belief line to every substantive piece of critical feedback for a month.

techniques.name: Say the uncomfortable thing early
techniques.summary: Unclear or delayed feedback is unkind; clarity early saves bigger problems later.
techniques.how_to_apply: Raise concerns at the first clear sign, briefly, rather than letting them build up.
techniques.drill: When Tom notices a concern, he raises it within the same week; the coach flags any feedback that lists three or more old examples.

techniques.name: Give credit publicly, by name
techniques.summary: Recognising individuals by name in front of peers reinforces the behaviour and signals what the leader values.
techniques.how_to_apply: In group settings, credit the specific person and what they did; avoid absorbing credit into 'we' or 'I'.
techniques.drill: In each team or stakeholder meeting, Tom names one person's contribution specifically.

techniques.name: Ask what's behind the position
techniques.summary: Positions are what people say they want; interests are why. Agreements are easier when built on interests.
techniques.how_to_apply: When someone takes a firm stance, ask 'what's driving that?' or 'what would that give you?', and note shared and different interests.
techniques.drill: In the next negotiation or stakeholder disagreement, Tom asks two interest questions before stating his own position.

techniques.name: Invent options for mutual gain
techniques.summary: Generate several options together before judging any, especially ones that trade on differences in priorities.
techniques.how_to_apply: Suggest a short brainstorm with no commitments, then look for trades where each side gets what it values most.
techniques.drill: In the next negotiation, Tom proposes at least three package options before settling.

techniques.name: Know your walk-away
techniques.summary: Being clear on your best alternative if no deal is struck protects against accepting a bad agreement or rejecting a good one.
techniques.how_to_apply: Before a negotiation, state aloud (in prep) your best alternative; in the room, compare offers to it rather than to your opening hope.
techniques.drill: Before each significant negotiation, Tom states his walk-away in a prep call with a colleague.

techniques.name: Use objective criteria
techniques.summary: Settle disagreements on fair standards (market data, precedent, expert view) rather than will.
techniques.how_to_apply: Ask 'what standard would be fair here?' and propose one; agree the standard before the number.
techniques.drill: In the next pricing or resourcing discussion, Tom proposes an external benchmark before giving a figure.

techniques.name: Ask how and what questions
techniques.summary: Open questions starting with 'how' or 'what' invite the other side to solve the problem with you and reveal constraints.
techniques.how_to_apply: Replace demands with questions like 'how would we make that work?' or 'what's the biggest obstacle on your side?'.
techniques.drill: In the next stakeholder negotiation, Tom replaces two demands with how/what questions.

techniques.name: Label the other side's concern
techniques.summary: Naming the emotion or concern you hear ('it sounds like...') can calm a tense exchange and show understanding.
techniques.how_to_apply: When you sense resistance, name it neutrally, then pause and let them respond.
techniques.drill: Use one label per tense conversation for two weeks; the coach checks the next turn for de-escalation.

techniques.name: Anticipate their objections aloud
techniques.summary: Naming the other side's likely objections first can lower defensiveness and make it easier to discuss them.
techniques.how_to_apply: Before your ask, list the concerns they may have ('you may think this is too late, too expensive...') and invite correction.
techniques.drill: Before the next difficult ask, Tom opens by naming two likely objections.

techniques.name: Pre-wire before the big meeting
techniques.summary: Talk to key stakeholders one-to-one before a group decision so surprises and objections surface early.
techniques.how_to_apply: In 1:1 soundings, share the draft recommendation, ask for concerns, and adjust; don't ask them to commit secretly.
techniques.drill: Before the next contentious proposal, Tom holds three pre-wire conversations including one likely opponent.

sources.where: find partners, keep the opposition close

techniques.name: Keep the opposition close
techniques.summary: Spend time with those most opposed, understand their losses, and acknowledge them, rather than only courting allies.
techniques.how_to_apply: Ask opponents what they stand to lose; acknowledge it explicitly; look for what could reduce it.
techniques.drill: Identify the most opposed stakeholder on Tom's top initiative and hold a listening conversation.

sources.where: keep the opposition close, acknowledge loss

techniques.name: Bring a recommendation, not just a problem
techniques.summary: When raising issues upward, bring options and a recommended course so the boss can decide quickly.
techniques.how_to_apply: Structure upward asks: issue, options, recommendation, what you need from them.
techniques.drill: For every upward meeting this month, Tom's first two minutes contain the ask and his recommendation.

techniques.name: No surprises: flag early
techniques.summary: Tell the boss or stakeholders about likely problems early, before they hear it elsewhere.
techniques.how_to_apply: Raise risks while they're still risks, with your current view of likelihood and what you're doing.
techniques.drill: Each week Tom names one risk to his boss or key stakeholder with a likelihood and a plan.

techniques.name: Frame it in their goals
techniques.summary: People are more persuaded by arguments tied to what they care about than by the persuader's reasons.
techniques.how_to_apply: Open with their priority, show how the proposal serves it, then give evidence and a concrete example.
techniques.drill: Before the next pitch to a stakeholder, Tom writes their top goal and opens with it.

techniques.name: Use consistency with their stated commitments
techniques.summary: People prefer to act in line with commitments they've made; linking a request to their stated values or past decisions is persuasive.
techniques.how_to_apply: Refer back to what the stakeholder has already said or committed to, and show how the ask follows from it.
techniques.drill: In the next influence attempt, Tom links his ask to one thing the stakeholder said previously.

techniques.name: Give first, ask later
techniques.summary: Helping others without being asked builds goodwill and a genuine basis for later requests.
techniques.how_to_apply: Offer specific help to peers' priorities in conversation; when asking later, the relationship carries it.
techniques.drill: Tom makes one unprompted offer of help to a peer or stakeholder each week.

techniques.name: Ask for advice, not just support
techniques.summary: Asking a stakeholder for advice tends to increase how competent they think you are and draws them into the solution.
techniques.how_to_apply: Ask a senior stakeholder for their advice on a specific part of the plan, then show you used it.
techniques.drill: For the next initiative, Tom asks two stakeholders for specific advice and reports back what he did with it.

techniques.name: Mine for hidden disagreement
techniques.summary: Teams avoid conflict to stay comfortable; the leader's job is to bring buried disagreement into the open.
techniques.how_to_apply: When agreement seems too easy, say so and ask who sees it differently; give permission for the conflict once it starts.
techniques.drill: Once per team meeting, Tom names a moment of possibly false harmony and asks for the dissenting view.

techniques.name: Give permission in the moment
techniques.summary: When people start to disagree productively, say explicitly that this is the debate you want, so they don't back off.
techniques.how_to_apply: Interrupt gently to affirm: 'This is good. Keep going.' Then let the debate run.
techniques.drill: When the coach detects disagreement between others, it checks whether Tom affirmed or shut it down.

techniques.name: Restore mutual purpose
techniques.summary: When a conversation turns defensive, step out of the content and re-establish the goal you both share.
techniques.how_to_apply: Notice silence or attack; pause; state the shared goal; ask if they agree with it before returning to the issue.
techniques.drill: In the next tense exchange, Tom names the shared goal before continuing; the coach checks the other person's next turn.

techniques.name: Contrast: what I don't mean and what I do
techniques.summary: Clarifying what you don't mean before saying what you do helps prevent the other person hearing an attack.
techniques.how_to_apply: When a message could be misread, say 'I'm not saying X; I am saying Y'.
techniques.drill: In each difficult feedback conversation, Tom uses one contrasting statement where misreading is likely.

techniques.name: Start with facts, offer the story tentatively
techniques.summary: Begin hard conversations with observable facts, share your interpretation as a possibility, and ask for theirs.
techniques.how_to_apply: Order: what I saw, what I'm starting to conclude, how do you see it? Use tentative wording on the conclusion.
techniques.drill: For the next difficult conversation, Tom plans facts, story and question in that order; the coach checks the order.

techniques.name: Ask for their story first
techniques.summary: Inviting the other person's account early, and listening fully, reduces defensiveness and often changes the picture.
techniques.how_to_apply: Ask an open question about how they see it and paraphrase back before responding.
techniques.drill: In each conflict conversation, Tom paraphrases the other's view and gets a 'yes' before giving his own.

techniques.name: Name the emotion, then the issue
techniques.summary: Acknowledging feelings plainly lowers the temperature and lets the conversation move to the issue.
techniques.how_to_apply: Reflect the emotion you hear in neutral words, pause, then return to the substance.
techniques.drill: Practise one emotion acknowledgement per difficult conversation; the coach checks the other person's next turn.

techniques.name: Allow pauses after hard news
techniques.summary: After delivering difficult news, leaving silence lets the other person respond rather than being talked over.
techniques.how_to_apply: Say the hard thing, then stop. Wait for them before adding explanation.
techniques.drill: After delivering bad news, Tom waits for the other person to speak first; the coach checks who broke the silence.

techniques.name: Side by side against the problem
techniques.summary: Frame the conflict as both people versus the problem, not versus each other.
techniques.how_to_apply: Use joint language ('how do we solve this?') and describe the problem as external and shared.
techniques.drill: In the next disagreement, Tom reframes once as 'us versus the problem'.

techniques.name: Avoid 'you always', 'you never'
techniques.summary: Absolute words about people escalate conflict and invite counterexamples instead of change.
techniques.how_to_apply: Replace generalisations with a specific recent example and its effect.
techniques.drill: The coach flags absolutes in Tom's conflict turns for a month.

techniques.name: Raise the elephant early
techniques.summary: Raise the difficult topic early in the conversation rather than leaving it to the last minutes or not at all.
techniques.how_to_apply: Plan the one hard point and say it in the first few minutes, after a brief opening.
techniques.drill: Before each difficult conversation, Tom names the topic to the coach; the coach checks when it was raised.

techniques.name: Disagree upward respectfully
techniques.summary: Leaders also need to challenge decisions above them, clearly and with reasons, before committing.
techniques.how_to_apply: State the disagreement, reasons and what would change your mind; then commit if the decision stands.
techniques.drill: In the next meeting with a senior stakeholder where Tom disagrees, he states it with reasons in the meeting.

techniques.name: Move to action at the end
techniques.summary: Difficult conversations should end with who will do what, by when, and how follow-up happens; otherwise agreement evaporates.
techniques.how_to_apply: Summarise what you agreed, the actions and owners, and when you'll check in.
techniques.drill: Close every difficult conversation with an action summary; the coach checks the last minute.

techniques.name: Apologise when you've caused harm
techniques.summary: A brief, sincere apology for your own part restores safety faster than defending intent.
techniques.how_to_apply: Name what you did, its impact, and what you'll do differently; don't add 'but'.
techniques.drill: When the coach detects a conflict that Tom contributed to, it checks for a specific apology in the next conversation with that person.

techniques.name: Name the meeting type and output
techniques.summary: Different meetings (decision, problem-solving, update, 1:1) need different structures; mixing them muddles both.
techniques.how_to_apply: At the start, say the type and the output ('this is a decision meeting; we leave with a yes or no on X') and who decides.
techniques.drill: For two weeks, Tom opens each meeting he chairs with type, output and decider; the coach checks the first two minutes.

techniques.name: Frame agenda items as questions
techniques.summary: Agenda items phrased as questions to answer focus discussion better than topic labels.
techniques.how_to_apply: Turn 'Pricing' into 'Should we raise prices in Q1, and by how much?' and read the question out at the start of the item.
techniques.drill: Tom rewrites his next three agendas as questions and reads each one out.

techniques.name: Keep tactical and strategic separate
techniques.summary: Weekly tactical meetings should handle near-term issues; big strategic topics deserve their own time rather than being squeezed in.
techniques.how_to_apply: When a strategic topic surfaces in a tactical meeting, park it explicitly to a dedicated session with a date and owner.
techniques.drill: The coach checks parked topics resurface in a later recording within a month.

techniques.name: Round-robin on key items
techniques.summary: Hearing briefly from everyone on important items brings out unshared information and reduces dominance by a few voices.
techniques.how_to_apply: Go round the room with a time limit ('30 seconds each'), starting with the most junior, before open discussion.
techniques.drill: In each team meeting, run at least one round-robin; the coach checks the number of distinct speakers on that item.

techniques.name: Invite the quiet expert by name
techniques.summary: Specific invitations to people with relevant knowledge, especially those who've not spoken, surface information that otherwise stays hidden.
techniques.how_to_apply: Name the person and ask a specific, answerable question tied to their expertise.
techniques.drill: The coach lists participants with no turns after each meeting; Tom invites at least one by name next time.

techniques.name: Keep the leader's airtime in check
techniques.summary: When the most senior person dominates airtime, others contribute less and the group's information pool shrinks; dominant talkers also overrate the meeting.
techniques.how_to_apply: Watch Tom's share of talk against the fair share for the meeting; shorten turns; end turns with a question.
techniques.drill: The coach reports Tom's talk share vs fair share after every team meeting; aim to be within 1.5 times fair share in discussion meetings.

techniques.name: Redirect complaint cycles to action
techniques.summary: In team meetings, complaining loops are linked to worse outcomes while solution and action talk goes with better ones.
techniques.how_to_apply: When problem-talk repeats, acknowledge it and ask 'what can we do about it this week?'.
techniques.drill: The coach flags complaint chains of three or more turns; Tom practises redirecting within one turn of the flag.

techniques.name: Prioritise and execute under pressure
techniques.summary: When many problems hit at once, pick the most important one, focus the group on it, then move to the next.
techniques.how_to_apply: Say 'we can't solve all of these now; the one that matters most is X', and focus discussion there.
techniques.drill: In the next overloaded meeting, Tom names the single most important issue before any discussion.

techniques.name: Summarise as you go
techniques.summary: Periodic short summaries keep the group aligned, show listening and make the decision point visible.
techniques.how_to_apply: Every 10-15 minutes, summarise where the group has got to and what's still open.
techniques.drill: The coach counts mid-meeting summaries; aim for one per major item.

techniques.name: Agree what we'll tell others
techniques.summary: Leadership teams should leave each meeting agreeing what to cascade to their teams, so messages are consistent.
techniques.how_to_apply: In the last minutes, ask: 'What are we each telling our teams, and what stays in the room?'
techniques.drill: Add the cascade question to the close of every leadership meeting for a month.

techniques.name: Recap decisions, owners and dates
techniques.summary: End each meeting with a spoken recap of what was decided and who is doing what by when.
techniques.how_to_apply: Reserve the last three minutes; read back decisions and actions; ask 'what have I missed?'.
techniques.drill: The coach checks the last three minutes of each meeting for a recap with owners and dates.

techniques.name: Questions first on a pre-read
techniques.summary: When people have read a proposal beforehand (or in the first minutes), discussion can start from questions rather than a presentation.
techniques.how_to_apply: Circulate the paper, or give silent reading time, then open with 'questions and challenges' instead of presenting slides.
techniques.drill: For the next three proposal meetings, Tom does no presentation and opens with questions.

techniques.name: Same standing review each week
techniques.summary: Reviewing the same small set of measures and commitments in a fixed order makes problems visible early and accountability routine.
techniques.how_to_apply: Keep a fixed opening sequence (actions, three metrics, risks) each week, then new items.
techniques.drill: Fix the opening sequence for Tom's weekly team meeting and keep it for six weeks.

techniques.name: Frame the work as uncertain
techniques.summary: When the leader says openly that the work is new and uncertain, people see speaking up as part of the job rather than a risk.
techniques.how_to_apply: Open projects or discussions by naming what's unknown and why everyone's input is needed.
techniques.drill: Tom opens each project kick-off with one sentence on what's unknown and one asking for challenge.

techniques.name: Say 'I don't know' and 'I was wrong'
techniques.summary: Leaders who admit limits and mistakes make it safer for others to do the same, which supports team learning.
techniques.how_to_apply: When you don't know, say so and ask who does; when you got something wrong, say so plainly and move on.
techniques.drill: Tom makes one genuine 'I don't know' or 'I was wrong' statement a week in team settings.

techniques.name: Model curiosity with genuine questions
techniques.summary: Asking genuine questions (ones you don't know the answer to) signals that others' knowledge matters.
techniques.how_to_apply: Ask questions that start from not knowing ('what are you seeing that I'm not?') rather than testing questions.
techniques.drill: In each meeting, Tom asks one question that starts with 'what am I missing?' or similar.

techniques.name: Thank the messenger
techniques.summary: How the leader reacts when someone raises a problem or mistake decides whether people will raise the next one.
techniques.how_to_apply: First response to bad news: thanks, then a forward-looking question. Hold frustration for later, if at all.
techniques.drill: The coach finds every bad-news moment and scores Tom's first response; aim for thanks + forward question every time.

techniques.name: Destigmatise failure
techniques.summary: Distinguish preventable errors, complex failures and intelligent experiments, and respond to each appropriately rather than punishing all failure.
techniques.how_to_apply: When something fails, ask which kind it was; celebrate intelligent failures and focus on learning, not blame.
techniques.drill: After each setback, Tom labels the failure type aloud before discussing it.

techniques.name: Ask directly for concerns
techniques.summary: Managerial openness (actively asking and responding) predicts whether people speak up more than general inspiring leadership does.
techniques.how_to_apply: Ask specific questions like 'what concerns you about this?' and 'what would you do differently?'; leave silence for answers.
techniques.drill: End every proposal discussion with a specific concern question and a ten-second wait.

techniques.name: Close the loop on input
techniques.summary: People speak up again when they see their input acted on, or hear why it wasn't.
techniques.how_to_apply: Refer back to suggestions people made and say what happened to them.
techniques.drill: Each month, Tom names two suggestions from his team in a meeting and what happened to them.

techniques.name: Avoid the accidental diminisher moves
techniques.summary: Well-meaning habits (always having ideas, rescuing, being always on, quick answers) can shrink others' contribution.
techniques.how_to_apply: Notice when Tom jumps in with ideas, rescues people or speaks after every turn; deliberately hold back.
techniques.drill: The coach reports the share of other speakers' turns immediately followed by Tom; aim to reduce it.

techniques.name: Report back on your own commitments
techniques.summary: Trust rests on ability, benevolence and integrity; keeping and reporting on your own promises is visible integrity.
techniques.how_to_apply: When you commit to something in a meeting, report back on it unprompted next time, including when you've missed it.
techniques.drill: The coach tracks Tom's spoken commitments and checks for an unprompted report-back in the next recording.

techniques.name: Explain changes of course
techniques.summary: When plans or decisions change, explaining what changed and why keeps credibility; silent reversals feel arbitrary.
techniques.how_to_apply: Name the change, the new information, and what it means for people.
techniques.drill: Each time Tom changes a prior decision, the coach checks for the what-changed-and-why pattern.

techniques.name: Show genuine care for the person
techniques.summary: Leaders who show care for people as people earn the trust that makes direct challenge possible.
techniques.how_to_apply: Ask about what matters to the person, remember it, and respond to life events with flexibility.
techniques.drill: Tom follows up on one personal detail per 1:1 for a month.

techniques.name: Take the blame, give the credit
techniques.summary: Leaders who absorb blame outward and pass credit to the team build loyalty and safety.
techniques.how_to_apply: In front of seniors or clients, use 'I' for problems and name team members for successes.
techniques.drill: In each upward or client meeting, the coach checks pronouns in failure and success talk.

techniques.name: Match style to the moment
techniques.summary: Effective leaders shift among styles (visionary, coaching, affiliative, democratic, and occasionally directive) as situations demand; pacesetting and commanding styles hurt climate when overused.
techniques.how_to_apply: Name the moment: crisis needs direction, a new direction needs vision, a skilled team needs consultation. Notice when Tom defaults to setting the pace himself.
techniques.drill: After each meeting, the coach labels Tom's dominant style and Tom checks whether it fit the situation.

techniques.name: Create urgency honestly
techniques.summary: Major change starts with enough people believing change is needed now; leaders build that by sharing real data and customer reality.
techniques.how_to_apply: Share unvarnished facts about the threat or opportunity and invite people to see it for themselves; don't invent a crisis.
techniques.drill: In the next change discussion, Tom shares one piece of hard evidence and asks the team to draw the conclusion.

techniques.name: Run decisions as conflicts of ideas, not people
techniques.summary: High-performing leadership teams argue hard about ideas, then align; the leader keeps the fight on the issue.
techniques.how_to_apply: Ask people to argue the other side's case first, then their own; stop personal remarks immediately.
techniques.drill: In the next disagreement, Tom asks each side to state the other's case before arguing.

techniques.name: Level 5: ambition for the work, not yourself
techniques.summary: Collins described top leaders as combining personal humility with intense resolve for the organisation; the causal claim is disputed.
techniques.how_to_apply: In conversation, keep the focus on the organisation's results and others' contributions, and pair it with unwavering standards.
techniques.drill: The coach tracks 'I' vs 'we/they' in Tom's success talk for a month.

techniques.name: Lead by asking, not telling (coach mindset)
techniques.summary: Great managers act as coaches: they ask, listen and help people find answers, rather than direct every move.
techniques.how_to_apply: In 1:1s and problem-solving moments, use a question first and offer direction only when needed.
techniques.drill: The coach reports ask:tell for each 1:1; Tom aims for more questions than statements.

techniques.name: Tell one concrete story
techniques.summary: A single specific example, especially about a customer or colleague, often moves people more than abstract data alone.
techniques.how_to_apply: Pair the key number with one real, short story that shows what it means.
techniques.drill: For the next persuasive pitch, Tom pairs his main statistic with one 30-second story.
